summary.text: Shoreline landforms are the shapes of the coast, the strip where land meets the sea or a lake.
Their form depends on the lie of the land, on erosion by waves, and on the rock and soil the shore is made of.
Tides set how far up the shore sediment is dropped or worn away, and coasts with big tides lack barrier islands and lagoons.

facts.label: Coastline paradox
facts.value: Coasts keep changing, so exact length can't be fixed

items.prompt: The same big storm waves hit two coasts. One has a long, gently spread beach; the other rises in steep rock walls right at the water. Where does wave energy have the least room to spread out?

options.label: The wide, open shore
The cliffed shore
Both about the same
Neither, as tides absorb it

items.explain: Longer shores give waves more room to disperse their energy, while cliffs and short shore faces leave little room.

items.prompt: A coast has a tidal range of 6 metres and funnel-shaped estuaries. Which feature would you NOT expect to find there?

options.label: Sand ridges lined up with tidal currents
Water that rises and falls a lot
Barrier islands sheltering lagoons
Estuaries that widen toward the sea

items.explain: A range above 4 m makes it a macrotidal coast, and macrotidal coasts lack barrier islands and lagoons.

items.prompt: A surfer notices that bigger waves seem to reshape the beach more. Why?

options.label: Bigger waves bring more salt to dissolve rock
Bigger waves raise the tide much higher
Bigger waves only hit at low tide
Bigger waves release more energy and move more sediment

items.explain: Waves erode a coast as they break and release energy; the larger the wave, the more energy and the more sediment it moves.

items.prompt: Two mapmakers measure the same coastline and get different lengths. What basic problem are they running into?

options.label: Coasts keep changing, so no exact length exists
Satellites cannot see the shoreline
Coastlines are defined only by law
Tides make every map unreadable

items.explain: Because coasts are constantly changing, a coastline's exact perimeter cannot be determined, a problem called the coastline paradox.

items.prompt: On their own, how do ordinary tides usually affect the shore?

options.label: They are the main force cutting cliffs
They set where sediment is dropped or worn away
They have no effect on shore shape
They build barrier islands on every coast

items.explain: Tides do not typically erode by themselves, but they often determine the range over which sediment is deposited or eroded.

items.prompt: Two coasts are made of different rock, but the same waves strike both. Why might they end up as very different kinds of shore?

options.label: Waves ignore what a shore is made of
Only the tides decide shore type
Their rock and soil set what forms
Shore type depends only on nearby wildlife

items.explain: The geological composition of rock and soil dictates the type of shore that forms.
